Blast
BLAST
noun (Silent Generation slang)
From Old English blæst, a blowing, a gust of wind. The older English senses — a gust of wind, the sound of a trumpet, a blight, the explosion of powder — are centuries old; Webster’s 1828 verb meant to blight, to strike with a loud blast, or to split rocks with powder. The slang sense — a wild party or a great time ("We had a blast") — is American and recorded by the 1950s, from the idea of an explosion of fun. It became one of the most durable words the Silent Generation passed down.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

When a girl came home from the church hayride in 1957 and said "We had a blast," she meant they had laughed all the way there and sung all the way back. It is a good thing to have a blast, and Scripture does not frown on it: God "giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17), and there is "a time to laugh… and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). The older word reminds us who owns the real blast. In the Bible a blast is God’s breath or His trumpet. At the Red Sea Moses sang, "with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together" (Exo 15:8). At Jericho the walls fell at a long blast of the ram’s horn (Jos 6:5). Fun is a gift, but it makes a poor god. Solomon tried to live for it and found it empty: "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). Paul warned of a day when men would be "lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God" (2Ti 3:4). So a grandfather can say both things: have a blast, children — laugh, sing, play ball till dark. But keep the fun in its place, under God, and remember that one day the last trumpet will sound its own great blast, and those who love Christ will enter a joy that never ends.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s) for a great time or a wild party ("we had a blast") — from the 1828 blast of wind or trumpet, and a word Scripture lets us enjoy under the God who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1Ti 6:17).

expand to see more

BLAST, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A great time; an exciting party or outing. "The church hayride was a blast."

Webster (1828) — BLAST, verb transitive [Literally, to strike.] To make to wither by some pernicious influence, as too much heat or moisture, or other destructive cause; or to check growth and prevent from coming to maturity and producing fruit; to blight, as trees or plants. 2. To confound, or strike with force, by a loud blast or din. 3. To split rocks by an explosion of gun powder.

Decode for families: "had a blast" means "had a great time" — no explosives, and no cursing (the old exclamation blast it! is a different use).

Key Scripture

Exo 15:8 — "And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea."

Ecc 3:4 — "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;"

Ecc 2:2 — "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?"

1Ti 6:17 — "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;"

2Ti 3:4 — "Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;"

Modern Corruption

A cheerful word for a good time; the only danger is the old one of loving pleasure more than God, or calling a sinful party a blast.

expand to see more

Having a blast is not a sin; Scripture gives us laughter, feasts, and dancing in their season. The word itself is clean, and most of the blasts our grandparents remembered were picnics, dances, and road trips.

The caution is twofold. First, fun can become a god, and a life arranged around the next blast is the life Paul described (2Ti 3:4). Second, the world often calls a blast what God calls drunkenness or lust; the word can dress up sin as a good time. A Christian family can have a blast together and still teach children to ask whether the fun is the kind they could thank God for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English blæst (a blowing) → English blast (gust, trumpet sound, blight, explosion) → 1950s slang (a great time) → lasting everyday English.

Old English blæst — a blowing, a gust, a breath

English blast — a gust of wind; the sound of a trumpet; a blight; an explosion

Biblical: the blast of God’s nostrils (Exo 15:8); the ram’s horn at Jericho (Jos 6:5)

1950s American slang: a blast — a great time, a party

Usage

""We drove to the shore in Uncle Ed’s Buick, eight of us crammed in. What a blast.""

"A time to weep, and a time to laugh (Ecc 3:4)."

"Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice (Php 4:4)."
